questions.q: When Get-Process | Select-Object -First 3 prints what looks like a plain text table, what is actually happening?
options: PowerShell is auto-formatting real objects for display — the underlying object with its full properties is still there
The pipeline has already converted everything to permanent plain text
Select-Object deletes every property except the ones shown in the console
PowerShell cannot display objects at all, only text
questions.explain: What prints to the console is a display convenience; it doesn't change that real, queryable properties still exist on the object.

questions.q: What does Get-Member prove about the objects Get-Process returns?
options: That real, queryable properties like CPU, Id, and ProcessName exist whether or not they appear as a console column
That Get-Process returns plain strings with no properties
That every property is identical across all processes
That Get-Member only works after using Format-Table first
questions.explain: Get-Member lists the object's real TypeName and every property and method available, regardless of what the console chose to display.

questions.q: What actually happens when you pipe objects into Format-Table?
options: The pipeline is converted into display-only formatting instruction objects, not the original objects anymore
Nothing changes — Format-Table is purely cosmetic and has no effect on the pipeline
Format-Table deletes the objects entirely and returns nothing
Format-Table converts every property into a new data type automatically
questions.explain: This is why Format-* cmdlets should be the last thing in a pipeline — what comes out isn't usable as the original object anymore.

questions.q: Why does parsing Format-Table's -AutoSize text output break in a way that Select-Object Name, CPU does not?
options: AutoSize column widths shift based on the widest value in the current results, so text parsing built on fixed widths breaks silently
Format-Table -AutoSize always produces exactly the same column widths every time, so parsing it is perfectly safe
Select-Object cannot be used with the CPU property
There is no meaningful difference between the two approaches
questions.explain: Column widths in AutoSize output depend on the current batch of data, making text-parsing fragile — reading the real property does not have that problem.

questions.q: What is the real rule this lesson lands on for working with pipelines?
options: Work with objects through every stage of a pipeline and only format for display at the very end
Always use Format-Table as the first cmdlet in every pipeline
Never use Get-Member in a real script
Text parsing is always safer than working with object properties
questions.explain: Formatting should come last, right before output is meant for a human to read — everything before that should work with real object properties.
